description: Pacifism, non-violent action and how religious individuals and communities work for peace.
content_html:
What Is Pacifism?

Pacifism is the principled rejection of violence as a means of resolving conflict. It is one of the most significant positions in religious ethics, rooted in teachings about the sanctity of life, the command to love others, and the belief that peace — rather than victory in war — is the true goal. Not all pacifists hold the same position, however, and it is important to distinguish between the two main forms.

Absolute pacifism holds that violence is always wrong, regardless of the circumstances. Absolute pacifists believe that no military objective, however worthy, justifies the taking of human life. This position is most strongly associated with the Quakers, who issued a famous declaration in 1660 stating that they would “utterly deny all outward wars and strife, and fightings with outward weapons, for any end, or under any pretence whatsoever.” This Quaker Declaration of 1660 remains one of the clearest statements of absolute pacifism in religious history.

Conditional pacifism accepts that violence is deeply undesirable and should be avoided, but allows that in extreme situations — for example, stopping genocide or defending the innocent — force may be the lesser evil. Many mainstream Christians occupy this position: they believe war is tragic and should be a last resort, but do not rule it out absolutely. The distinction between absolute and conditional pacifism is important for exam questions asking you to compare different religious attitudes to violence.

Pacifism in the Sermon on the Mount

The Sermon on the Mount contains some of the most demanding ethical teachings in Christianity and is a cornerstone for Christian pacifists. In Matthew 5:38–42, Jesus explicitly challenges the ancient principle of “an eye for an eye”: “But I tell you, do not resist an evil person. If anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to them the other cheek also.” This teaching on turning the other cheek is not generally read as passive submission to abuse; rather, it is interpreted as a form of dignified, non-violent resistance that refuses to repay violence with violence.

Matthew 5:43–44 extends this further: “You have heard that it was said, ‘Love your neighbour and hate your enemy.’ But I tell you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.” For many Christians, this command to love enemies is the foundation of pacifism — if you genuinely love someone, you cannot wish harm on them, even if they are doing you harm.

Key Fact

The Quaker Declaration of 1660 states that Quakers “utterly deny all outward wars and strife, and fightings with outward weapons, for any end, or under any pretence whatsoever.” It is the classic expression of absolute pacifism in English religious history and is directly cited in the specification for this topic.

Non-Violent Action: Key Figures

Non-violent action is the active use of peaceful methods to resist injustice and work for change. It is different from passivity — it involves deliberate, sustained effort to challenge unjust systems without employing violence. Three figures are central to this tradition in the 20th century:

Mahatma Gandhi developed the philosophy of satyagraha (truth-force or soul-force) in South Africa and India. He led mass campaigns of civil disobedience — strikes, boycotts and peaceful marches — against British colonial rule. Gandhi drew on Hindu teachings about ahimsa (non-violence) as well as on Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount. He demonstrated that non-violent resistance could achieve major political goals and inspire movements worldwide.

Martin Luther King Jr led the American civil rights movement in the 1950s and 1960s. A Baptist minister, King was deeply influenced by both Gandhi’s methods and by Jesus’s teaching to love enemies. He organised bus boycotts, sit-ins and marches to challenge racial segregation, explicitly rejecting violence even when attacked. His famous “Letter from Birmingham Jail” argues that non-violent direct action forces the community to confront its injustice and creates a creative tension that leads to negotiation and change.

Desmond Tutu, an Anglican Archbishop in South Africa, used his faith to oppose apartheid and later to chair the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. Like King, Tutu argued that Christian love required active opposition to injustice — but without hatred for the oppressor. He stressed that the goal was not to defeat enemies but to transform them and restore community.

Key Fact

Gandhi (Hindu-inspired ahimsa), Martin Luther King Jr (Baptist Christian, love of enemies) and Desmond Tutu (Anglican Christian, reconciliation) are the three named individuals in the specification for this lesson. Each rooted their non-violent activism in religious conviction, not merely political strategy.

Organisations Working for Peace

Religious and ethical organisations have also worked collectively for peace. The CCND — more commonly known as CND (Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament) — was founded in Britain in 1957 and draws support from religious believers as well as secular humanists. It argues that nuclear weapons can never be morally justified and campaigns for multilateral disarmament. Many faith communities, including Quakers and several Catholic organisations, have supported CND campaigns on the grounds that nuclear weapons are incompatible with any just war criteria.

Beyond formal organisations, religious communities work for peace in many everyday ways: through prayer for peace, through reconciliation programmes between conflicting groups, through education about the causes of violence, and through practical aid to communities torn apart by conflict. Whether working for peace should be the most important activity for believers is itself a matter of theological debate: some Christians argue that evangelism (spreading the gospel) is the primary calling; others argue that working for justice and peace is central to following Jesus.

Critics of pacifism argue that it can be ineffective or even irresponsible. If an aggressor is not deterred by peaceful protest, non-violent resistance may simply allow injustice to continue unchallenged. The philosopher Reinhold Niebuhr argued that Christians who refuse all force are failing their responsibility to protect the innocent. He called this position “irresponsible perfectionism.” However, defenders of pacifism argue that violence often escalates conflict rather than resolving it, that it corrupts those who use it, and that non-violent methods — as Gandhi and King demonstrated — can achieve profound social change. They also argue that Christian ethics requires living out the Kingdom of God’s values now, even if it appears impractical.
exam_tip_html: For the 15-mark “Discuss” on pacifism, you need to present both absolute and conditional pacifist positions, not just argue one side. Name specific individuals (Gandhi, Martin Luther King, Desmond Tutu, Quaker Declaration 1660) and specific teachings (Matthew 5:38–42, Matthew 5:43–44). The most common error is treating all pacifists as holding the same view — examiners want to see you distinguish absolute from conditional pacifism. Spell “pacifism” and “non-violence” correctly; SPaG is assessed on your extended response.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Absolute pacifism holds that violence is always wrong (Quakers, Declaration 1660); conditional pacifism allows that force may sometimes be a tragic last resort — these are importantly different positions.
  • Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:38–42 and 5:43–44) is the key Christian scriptural foundation for pacifism and non-violent resistance.
  • Gandhi, Martin Luther King Jr and Desmond Tutu each used religious conviction as the basis for non-violent action against injustice, demonstrating that pacifism can be an active, not merely passive, stance.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by 'absolute pacifism'.
practice_questions.marks: The belief that violence is always wrong in all circumstances and without exception. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which religious individuals or communities have worked for peace.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for two distinct points, for example: Martin Luther King Jr organised peaceful protests and marches to oppose racial segregation in the USA, drawing on his Christian faith; Quaker communities have actively campaigned with CND for nuclear disarmament, arguing nuclear weapons are morally unjustifiable. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline three religious teachings or sources that support pacifism.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three distinct points, for example: The Quaker Declaration of 1660 states that Quakers 'utterly deny all outward wars and strife, and fightings with outward weapons'; Jesus teaches 'love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you' (Matthew 5:43-44); Matthew 5:38-42 challenges the principle of revenge, teaching people to 'turn the other cheek'. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why some religious believers adopt an absolute pacifist position.
practice_questions.marks: Credit two developed points, for example: Jesus's teaching in the Sermon on the Mount commands love of enemies and non-retaliation (Matthew 5:38-44) — absolute pacifists argue that if you genuinely love someone you cannot kill them, and that Christian ethics must embody God's kingdom values here and now regardless of practical consequences (3 marks). The Quaker tradition, grounded in the belief that there is 'that of God in every person', holds that killing any human being destroys a divine spark — therefore no cause or authority can justify war; the 1660 Declaration is their founding statement of this absolute commitment (3 marks). [6 marks — 3 marks per reason: 1 basic, 2 developed, 3 developed with teaching]

practice_questions.text: 'Non-violent action is always the best way to achieve peace and justice.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: Gandhi's satyagraha campaigns achieved Indian independence without armed revolution; Martin Luther King's non-violent civil rights movement led to landmark legislation in the USA; the Sermon on the Mount teaches 'turn the other cheek' and 'love your enemies', suggesting that violence only perpetuates cycles of hatred; the Quaker Declaration 1660 argues all violence is a denial of God's presence in every person; non-violent action preserves the moral integrity of those using it.

Arguments against: Non-violent action is not always effective — it depends on an opponent who can be shamed or persuaded; against truly brutal regimes that simply massacre protesters, non-violence may allow injustice to continue; conditional pacifists argue force is sometimes the only way to protect the innocent; Just War Theory allows that some defensive wars are morally necessary; many religious believers do not accept absolute pacifism.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named individuals, scripture and theological argument; explicit weighing and justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides addressed with some named teachings and a conclusion.
Developing: Some attempt at both sides; limited evidence.
Emerging: One-sided or very brief; little or no religious teaching cited. [15 marks + SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Outline three differences between absolute pacifism and conditional pacifism.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three distinct differences: Absolute pacifism holds that violence is always wrong in every circumstance; conditional pacifism allows that violence may be a tragic last resort in extreme situations such as defending the innocent; absolute pacifists (such as Quakers) refuse to serve in any military capacity, whereas conditional pacifists may support just defensive wars. [3 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which religious group is most associated with absolute pacifism and issued a famous declaration in 1660?
Which passage in Matthew does Jesus teach 'turn the other cheek' and refuse to retaliate against evil?
The belief that violence is generally wrong but may be justified in extreme circumstances is called _____ pacifism.
Martin Luther King Jr was a Baptist minister who drew on both Gandhi's methods and Jesus's teaching to lead the _____ movement in the USA.
Match each person or group to their contribution to pacifism or peacemaking:
right: Led satyagraha campaigns against British colonial rule using ahimsa
Used non-violent protest to challenge racial segregation in the USA
Issued a declaration utterly denying all outward wars and strife

flashcard_questions.a: The belief that violence is always morally wrong, in all circumstances without exception.
The view that violence is wrong but may be a last resort when defending the innocent.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Quaker Declaration of 1660 state?
flashcard_questions.a: Quakers 'utterly deny all outward wars and strife, and fightings with outward weapons.'

flashcard_questions.q: What does Matthew 5:38-42 teach about retaliation?
flashcard_questions.a: Do not resist an evil person; if struck on the right cheek, turn the other cheek.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Matthew 5:43-44 say about enemies?
flashcard_questions.a: Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.

flashcard_questions.q: What philosophy of non-violence did Gandhi develop?
flashcard_questions.a: Satyagraha — truth-force or soul-force — rooted in the Hindu concept of ahimsa.
Using peaceful methods such as protest and civil disobedience to oppose injustice without force.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Martin Luther King Jr's Christian faith lead him to argue about racial segregation?
flashcard_questions.a: It must be opposed through non-violent direct action rooted in love of enemies.

flashcard_questions.q: What is CCND (CND) and what does it campaign for?
flashcard_questions.a: The Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament, which campaigns for the abolition of nuclear weapons.

flashcard_questions.q: How did Desmond Tutu contribute to peace in South Africa?
flashcard_questions.a: He opposed apartheid using his Christian faith and chaired the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Sermon on the Mount and where is it found?
flashcard_questions.a: Jesus's core ethical teachings recorded in Matthew chapters 5 to 7.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do critics argue that pacifism can be irresponsible?
flashcard_questions.a: If an aggressor is not deterred by peaceful protest, non-violence may allow injustice to continue.

glossary_terms.definition: The belief that violence and war are always wrong and that disputes should be settled by peaceful means.
The view that violence is always morally wrong, in all circumstances and without exception.
The view that violence is generally wrong but may be justified in extreme circumstances such as defending the innocent from grave harm.
A collection of Jesus's teachings recorded in Matthew chapters 5 to 7, including the Beatitudes and core ethical commands.
Using peaceful methods such as protest, boycott, civil disobedience and dialogue to oppose injustice without resorting to force.
The Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament, a UK organisation founded in 1957 that calls for the abolition of nuclear weapons and peaceful alternatives to conflict.
